Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

🇺🇸 Current (post-Elon X, H2 2024 / 2025 Transparency Report)

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

The Knights of Columbus (KOC) is a global Catholic fraternal service order founded by Blessed Michael J. McGivney. Membership is limited to practicing Catholic men. It is led by Patrick E. Kelly, the order's 14th Supreme Knight.

The organization was founded on March 29, 1882, as a mutual benefit society for working-class and immigrant Catholics in the United States. In addition to providing an insurance system for its members, it has grown to support refugee relief, Catholic education, local parishes and dioceses, and global Catholic social causes. The Knights of Columbus have played an active role in politics ever since its formation, and promote the Catholic view on public policy issues around the world.

The organization also provides certain financial services to the individual and institutional Catholic market. Its wholly owned insurance company, a Fortune 1000 company based on its annual revenue, underwrites more than two million insurance contracts, totaling more than $123 billion of life insurance in force as of 2025. The order also owns the Knights of Columbus Asset Advisors, a money management firm which invests in accordance with Catholic social teachings.

As of 2025, the Knights reported having over 2.2 million members around the world. Women may participate in KOC through the Columbiettes and other female auxiliaries, and boys may join the Columbian Squires. The Order comprises four different "degrees", each one of which exemplifies one of the core principles of the order. There are more than 17,000 local Knights of Columbus councils around the world, including over 400 on college campuses.

Organization and principles
The order is dedicated to the principles of charity, unity, fraternity, and patriotism.[44] Membership is restricted to men, at least 18 years of age, who are practicing Catholics in union with the Holy See and are in good standing with the Church.[45] As of October 2025, there were over 2.2 million Knights of Columbus worldwide, with the majority in North America.[46][47][48][49][50]

After his induction and completion of the Exemplification of Charity, a new member becomes a First Degree Knight. He then progresses through the Second and Third Degrees after completing the subsequent Exemplifications of Unity and Fraternity. A Third Degree Knight is considered to have attained full "Knighthood" status. Privileges of Third Degree membership include the ability to serve as a local council officer, and admission to state and Supreme Council business meetings.

A Third Degree Knight in good standing is eligible to complete the Exemplification of Patriotism and progress to the Fourth Degree. This is an optional degree, but represents the highest ideals of the order. A Knight who has attained this level is addressed as "Sir Knight".

Each member belongs to one of more than 17,000 local councils around the world.[47][51] Most are based in Catholic parishes, though some have their own council hall within a community. Each local council works to assist with the needs of its community consistent with the principles of the order.

The college councils program, started at Catholic University of America in 1898, was created to promote the moral, intellectual and spiritual development of college men on campuses throughout the world.[65] The oldest continuously running college council is the University of Notre Dame Council #1477, chartered in 1910.[66] Councils at seminaries ("seminarian councils") are classified as college councils. As of 2026, there are more than 37,000 knights at 320 college councils worldwide.[52]

Throughout most of its history, the Knights of Columbus has provided active support to members of the armed forces and their families. As of 2024, there are more than 50 military councils in military bases throughout North America and around the world.

A Knight who has attained the Fourth Degree also belongs to a Fourth Degree assembly. Fourth Degree Knights are men who have chosen to embrace the order's fourth principle of patriotism. Fourth Degree assemblies get their members from multiple councils within a local geographical area. They lead the efforts to reach out to veterans and active military and to embody the fact that one can be a faithful Catholic and also be a faithful citizen.[67] As of 2024, there are more than 3,600 Fourth Degree assemblies worldwide. The 125th anniversary of the Fourth Degree was celebrated in February 2025, presided over by Cardinal Timothy Dolan.[68]

Fourth Degree assemblies may form Color Corps, an elective division of the Fourth Degree, whose distinctive presence in parades, wreath-laying ceremonies, Confirmations and other Catholic functions are a visible reminder of the Knights' service to their communities. Fourth Degree Color Corps are often the most visible arm of the Knights.[69][70]

The Supreme Council is the governing body of the order. It elects insurance members to serve three-year terms on a 24-member Board of Directors.[71][72] Leaders' salaries are set by the board of directors and ratified by the delegates to the Supreme Convention.[73] The seven-figure salaries of senior KOC officers have been criticized as excessive.[73][74]

In 1969, the Knights opened a 23-story headquarters building in New Haven.[75][76]

Michael Joseph McGivney (August 12, 1852 – August 14, 1890) was an American Catholic priest based in New Haven, Connecticut. He founded the Knights of Columbus at a local parish to serve as a mutual aid and insurance organization, particularly for immigrants and their families. It developed through the 20th century as the world's largest Catholic fraternal organization.

The cause for his canonization started in the Archdiocese of Hartford in 1996; in March 2008, Pope Benedict XVI declared McGivney "Venerable" in recognition of his "heroic virtue".[1] On May 27, 2020, Pope Francis announced that McGivney had been approved for beatification, which officially occurred on October 31, 2020.[2]

Early life
Childhood and youth
Michael McGivney was born in Waterbury, Connecticut, on August 12, 1852, to Irish immigrant parents, Patrick and Mary (née Devine) McGivney. He was the eldest of 13 children, six of whom died in infancy or childhood. Patrick worked as a molder at a brass mill in Waterbury.

McGivney attended public school in Waterbury. Termed a well behaved and proficient student, he was able to graduate high school in 1865 at age 13. McGivney then started working in one of brass mills in Waterbury, making metal spoons.[3][4] While still a teenager, he decided that he wanted to become a priest.

Studies for the priesthood
In 1868, at age 16, McGivney entered the Séminaire de Saint-Hyacinthe in Saint-Hyacinthe, Quebec, in Canada. He continued his studies in 1871 at Our Lady of Angels Seminary in Lewiston, New York.[3]While at Our Lady, he and other seminarians formed a baseball team; McGivney was described as a "naturally talented ballplayer."[5]

A year later, in 1872, McGivney enrolled in the Collège Sainte-Marie de Montréal, operated by the Jesuits in Montreal, Quebec. Patrick McGivney died in 1873, forcing his son to leave Sainte-Marie.[6]At this point, he could not afford more seminary training. However, seeing McGivney's potential, Bishop Francis Patrick McFarland of the Diocese of Hartford elected to pay for the seminarian's remaining education at St. Mary's Seminary, in Baltimore, Maryland.

Establishing Knights of Columbus
During the second half of the 19th century, the Catholic hierarchy in the United States became concerned about Irish Catholic men joining extremist secret societies such as the Molly Maguires or the Fenian Brotherhood.[10]The bishops were very receptive to the creation of fraternal groups that embrace Catholic values and American patriotism. From his own experience, McGivney recognized the devastating effect on immigrant families of the father's untimely death. Many of these families were split, with the children suffering the loss of parents and estrangement from the Catholic Church.[6]

Blue laws (also known as Sunday laws, Sunday trade laws, and Sunday closing laws) are laws restricting or banning certain activities on specified days, usually Sundays in the western world. The laws were adopted originally for religious reasons, specifically to promote the observance of the Christian day of worship. Since then, they have come to serve secular purposes as well.

Blue laws commonly ban certain business and recreational activities on Sundays, and impose restrictions on the retail sale of hard goods and consumables, particularly alcoholic beverages.[1][2] The laws also place limitations on a range of other endeavors—including travel, fashions, hunting, professional sports, stage performances, movie showings, and gambling.[3][4] While less prevalent today, blue laws continue to be enforced in parts of the United States and Canada as well as in European countries, such as Austria, Germany, Norway, and Poland, where most stores are required to close on Sundays.[3][5][6][7][8]

In the United States, the Supreme Court has upheld blue laws as constitutional despite their religious origins if supported by secular justifications. This has resulted in the provision of a day of rest for the general population.[9][10] Meanwhile, various state courts have struck down the laws as either unenforceable or in violation of their states' constitutions. In response, state legislators have re-enacted certain Sunday laws to satisfy the rulings while allowing some of the other statutes to remain on the books with no intention to enforce them.[11][failed verification]

BCI Halted Advocate Enrolment of NALSAR’s 2026 Graduates, Withdrew Decision Within Hours

New Delhi Post | Legal News

The Bar Council of India (BCI) withdrew, within a few hours, its decision to halt the enrolment of NALSAR University of Law’s 2026 batch of law graduates as advocates. The BCI’s initial decision came after a campaign by students who objected to the invitation of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant as the Chief Guest at the university’s convocation.

BCI Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra, who is also a BJP Rajya Sabha MP, had initially directed that no student who obtained a law degree from NALSAR in 2026 should be enrolled as an advocate by any State Bar Council until further orders. The BCI also sought factual details and identification of the students who had organised the campaign opposing the CJI’s participation in the convocation.

The decision, however, triggered a sharp reaction from the legal community. Supreme Court Bar Association President Vikas Singh described the BCI’s initial action as arbitrary, illegal, disproportionate and fundamentally unsustainable. While he clarified that he did not support the students’ protest, he questioned the decision to collectively halt the enrolment of all students.

Following the backlash, the BCI modified its decision. Manan Kumar Mishra said the Council was of the view that the vast majority of NALSAR’s 2026 graduating students were innocent and had not intended to participate in any alleged move to show “disrespect” to the highest judicial office.

The BCI has now decided to await a formal inquiry report from the NALSAR Vice-Chancellor. A final decision in the matter is proposed to be taken on August 19.

How Did the Controversy Begin?

The controversy began with a campaign by NALSAR students, who on August 10 requested the university to reconsider its decision to invite CJI Surya Kant as the Chief Guest at the convocation.

The students objected to certain remarks made by CJI Surya Kant during a hearing on July 20. The matter concerned alleged police action against a student march towards Parliament. The petitioner had requested that video footage of the police action be examined, to which the CJI reportedly said that he did not have time to watch the videos.

NALSAR has not yet finalised the date of its convocation. The university has traditionally invited the CJI to its convocation ceremony.

Key Fact: The BCI initially halted the Advocate Enrolment of NALSAR’s 2026 graduates but withdrew the decision within a few hours. A final decision in the matter will now follow the inquiry report.

More Important Developments — August 14, 2026
Christians facing increased harassment in Israel

Christians, who constitute less than 2% of Israel’s population, report increasing incidents of spitting, vandalism and physical intimidation—particularly in Jerusalem’s Old City. A nun was recently assaulted, and Jewish volunteers have begun accompanying some Christian clergy for protection. Authorities say policing and penalties are being strengthened, but many Christians remain concerned about their future in the Holy Land. Associated Press

Massive oil spill threatening Oman

A grounded tanker carrying Russian crude has produced an oil slick covering approximately 2,000 square kilometers. Oil is reaching Oman’s coastline near a protected marine area, potentially affecting 25 miles of shoreline and damaging sea life, fishing communities and beaches. Regional conflict and questions concerning responsibility for the sanctioned tanker have complicated cleanup efforts. Reuters

European drought threatening nuclear power

Record-low water in the Danube River has deprived nuclear plants of sufficient cooling water. Romania shut its last operating reactor, while Hungary’s Paks plant is operating at only about 25% capacity. Hungary plans to sink two large barges near its plant to raise the immediate water level while constructing a longer-term barrier. This shows how prolonged drought can threaten electricity production as well as agriculture and drinking water. Reuters

Major companies investigating possible cyberattack

The Cl0p hacking group claims it stole data from nearly 50 companies, including Shell, Philips, GE and financial-technology company Fiserv. The companies are investigating, but Reuters has not independently confirmed the hackers’ claims or established that customer information was taken. It nevertheless illustrates the danger posed by one software vulnerability spreading through numerous major organizations. Reuters

More countries restricting children’s social media

Australia already prohibits social-media accounts for children younger than 16, while Britain, Spain, Denmark, Greece, Poland and other countries are considering or implementing similar limits. France’s highest constitutional court blocked its proposed under-15 ban today, ruling that its age-verification system threatened privacy and freedom of expression. Governments are struggling to balance children’s mental health and safety against privacy and free-speech rights. Reuters overview and French ruling

License-plate surveillance concerns in America

Flock Safety operates automatic license-plate cameras in 49 states. Following reports of unauthorized or questionable searches, it announced that police agencies must adopt auditing tools, connect searches to case numbers and shorten routine data retention from 30 days to seven. Critics say the cameras can help solve crimes but still allow authorities to track innocent people’s movements without judicial approval. Associated Press

Child labor discovered in an Indian supply chain

Indian authorities rescued four children, ages 14–16, who reportedly worked six days each week at an electrical-component supplier. Major manufacturer Eureka Forbes has begun auditing its supply chain, while authorities asked other companies named by the supplier to investigate. The case demonstrates how child labor can remain hidden several levels beneath familiar consumer brands. Reuters

Stingray encounters increasing along Southern California

Warmer coastal water is bringing more stingrays into shallow water. More than 3,100 stings have been reported this year at Bolsa Chica and Huntington State Beaches—twice last year’s total—and San Diego has recorded more than 900. This may also be worth remembering during your walks near Pismo Beach: if you enter shallow water, shuffle your feet instead of stepping normally so stingrays have time to move away. Most stings are treatable, but a deeply embedded barb or severe reaction needs medical attention. Associated Press

The most personally useful item for you is the stingray warning if you enter the ocean. The Christian harassment, oil spill, child labor and healthcare crises are especially worthwhile subjects for prayer and compassionate attention.

Childhood-vaccine policy dispute in America

President Trump has directed federal officials to explore separating combination vaccines such as MMR into individual injections given at different appointments. Major medical organizations oppose the proposal, saying the present schedule is supported by extensive research and that additional appointments could leave children unprotected longer. The order cannot compel manufacturers to produce discontinued single-disease vaccines or force states to change school requirements, so its practical effect remains uncertain. Associated Press

Serious strain aboard a U.S. aircraft carrier

The USS Abraham Lincoln has spent more than 260 days at sea supporting operations connected to the Iran war. Reports of supply shortages, crew exhaustion and mental-health difficulties have prompted congressional concern. The USS George Washington is traveling from the Pacific to relieve it, temporarily leaving the Pacific without an American aircraft carrier. The story reveals the human and strategic cost of maintaining a prolonged war. Associated Press

El Niño disrupting Pacific sea life

Seabirds normally found near Peru and Chile are appearing far north in Panama. Scientists say unusually warm water is driving anchovies and sardines away from their normal areas, forcing birds to travel much farther for food. The birds’ movement provided an early natural warning that a powerful El Niño was developing. This could eventually influence rainfall, storms, agriculture and fisheries around the Pacific—including California. Reuters

U.S.–Canada tariff deadline approaching

American and Canadian officials are attempting to complete a trade agreement before August 19, when President Trump has threatened 50% tariffs on certain Canadian products. Negotiators from both countries say discussions are progressing. An agreement would protect one of the world’s largest trading relationships and help prevent additional price increases for businesses and consumers. Reuters

China–New Zealand espionage dispute

New Zealand’s latest security assessment identifies China as the country’s most active source of foreign interference and large-scale espionage. China rejected the accusation as false and harmful to relations. The dispute is significant because New Zealand belongs to the Five Eyes intelligence alliance but also relies heavily upon trade with China. Reuters

India expanding access to nuclear energy

India is developing a tightly controlled approval process allowing private projects to use proven foreign reactor technology. India wants to increase nuclear capacity from roughly 9 gigawatts today to 100 gigawatts by 2047. If conducted safely, this could provide dependable low-carbon electricity for a rapidly growing population; regulatory strength and waste management will be crucial.

Financial markets remain resilient

Despite weaker consumer spending, elevated oil prices and international conflict, the S&P 500 closed at a record Thursday and remained close to that level Friday. Inflation data earlier in the week were somewhat more encouraging, reducing immediate fears of another interest-rate increase. Markets are not the same as the entire economy, but this is evidence that investors do not currently expect imminent economic collapse. Reuters

International cooperation stopped a child-abuse network

In a rare constructive example of cooperation between political rivals, American and Chinese law-enforcement agencies worked together to dismantle a multinational child-sexual-abuse-material network. Sixteen suspects were arrested in June. The broader relationship between the two countries remains tense, but this shows that governments can still cooperate where innocent lives are at stake. text:
A federal judge just ruled that Ghislaine Maxwell’s Epstein grand jury records must be made public, rejecting every objection she raised. Congress’s Epstein Files Transparency Act overrides grand jury secrecy rules. #OpDeathEaters 

----------------------------------------------------------

Federal grand jury material from the prosecution of Ghislaine Maxwell must be released to the public, a New York judge ruled on 11 August, rejecting every objection Maxwell raised to keeping it sealed.
U.S. District Judge Loretta Preska found that the Epstein Files Transparency Act overrides the secrecy orders that have covered the material since Maxwell's 2021 conviction, and that the statute establishes the compelling need federal courts require before grand jury material is opened.

Maxwell's filings against disclosure amounted to "a veritable kitchen sink of objections," Preska wrote, running through procedural, statutory and constitutional grounds, all of which she found meritless. Release will carry the victim-protecting redactions the Act authorises.

What comes out
Grand jury subpoenas and material gathered by the government during the federal investigation into Jeffrey Epstein fall within the order, together with depositions taken from Maxwell in April and July 2016 in the civil defamation case Virginia Giuffre brought against her.

Prosecutors built two perjury counts in Maxwell's federal indictment on those 2016 depositions, charging her with lying under oath when she denied knowing about Epstein's recruitment and abuse of girls. The counts were later dismissed.

Records held by the law firm Boies Schiller Flexner, which represented Giuffre, are covered by the ruling.
Giuffre died in April 2025. Her allegations against Prince Andrew, which he has denied, cost him his royal titles and, on 18 February 2026, brought his arrest on suspicion of misconduct in public office over the alleged sharing of confidential documents with Epstein.

The statute against Rule 6(e)
Grand jury secrecy in the federal system runs on Rule 6(e) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which permits disclosure only in narrow circumstances and has historically defeated attempts to open Epstein-related material. Two federal judges refused Justice Department applications to unseal Epstein and Maxwell grand jury records in 2025 on exactly that ground.

Public Law 119-38 changed the calculation. Signed on 19 November 2025, it directs the Attorney General to publish all unclassified Justice Department records on Epstein and Maxwell, permits withholding only for victim identity, child sexual abuse material, active investigations, images of death or injury and classified national security material, and expressly bars withholding for embarrassment, reputational harm or political sensitivity.

Preska's reading treats the Act as a congressional finding of public need that displaces the earlier secrecy orders rather than as a request the court may weigh against them.

Maxwell's position
Maxwell is serving 20 years, imposed in June 2022 after a jury convicted her in December 2021 on rape trafficking and conspiracy counts for recruiting and grooming girls for Epstein.

She was moved from a federal prison in Florida to a minimum security federal prison camp in Texas in the summer of 2025, after two days of interviews with Todd Blanche, then Deputy Attorney General and now Attorney General. A Bureau of Prisons whistleblower has since given House Judiciary Democrats evidence of preferential treatment at the camp.

Maxwell filed an application for commutation with the Trump administration in November 2025. Her Supreme Court appeal was rejected in 2025.
Appearing under subpoena at a House Oversight Committee deposition on 9 February 2026, Maxwell invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to answer. 

Her lawyer David Oscar Markus said afterwards: "Maxwell is prepared to speak fully and honestly if granted clemency by President Trump." Her legal team has said she could explain why Trump and Bill Clinton are innocent of wrongdoing in connection with Epstein.

The Senate vote
The Senate adopted a resolution opposing any pardon or commutation for Maxwell on 29 July 2026, by unanimous consent, with no senator objecting. Senator Jacky Rosen brought it.

"Sexual predators should not be afforded preferential treatment," Senator Jack Reed said of the administration's handling of Maxwell.

Unanimous consent means no Republican senator objected, six days before the Judiciary Committee advanced Blanche's nomination on 4 August and 10 days before he won a floor vote 50 to 49.

Senate resolutions of this kind carry no legal force. Presidential clemency is not reviewable by the courts, and Trump could commute Maxwell's sentence at any point, including after the grand jury material becomes public.

🤔On August 12, 2026, the President of the United States signed a document that created something that didn't exist the day before.

The National Security Presidential Memorandum is titled "Expanding Capabilities to Combat Transnational Cyber-Enabled Crime." What it actually does is authorize vetted American private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations break-ins, disruption, sabotage against foreign criminal networks, under direct federal government oversight.

Read that again. Private companies. Offensive operations. Against foreign targets. Authorized by the President.

For the first time in American history, the federal government has formally deputized the private sector to attack.

Here's some history.

Article I, Section 8 of the United States Constitution grants Congress the power to "grant Letters of Marque and Reprisal." In the age of sail, a letter of marque was a government license authorizing a private ship to attack enemy vessels. The private captain operated under his own flag, with his own crew, at his own risk but with the legal authority of the sovereign behind him. He wasn't a pirate. He was a privateer. The difference was the piece of paper.

Letters of marque were how small nations punched above their weight at sea. You didn't need a massive navy if you could authorize your merchant fleet to fight. The private sector was faster, more innovative, and more numerous than any government fleet. All it needed was permission.

The United States just issued the digital equivalent.

The NSPM creates two categories of authorized private action.

The first is Cyber Surveillance Operations — gathering intelligence on foreign criminal networks, mapping their infrastructure, identifying their operators.

The second is Cyber Effects Operations. "Effects" is the government's word for disruption, degradation, and sabotage. Breaking things. Shutting systems down. Making the enemy's tools stop working.

Both categories are conducted under the direction, control, and authority of the federal government. The private companies don't freelance. They propose operations to the National Coordination Center, which sits under the Homeland Security Task Force and is run by two Executive Directors from the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security. The operations are reviewed, approved, and overseen by federal authorities. The Homeland Security Council establishes the procedures.

The private company provides the capability. The government provides the authority. Together they do what neither could do alone.

The predicate is a number: $20.8 billion.

That's how much Americans lost to cyber-enabled crime in 2025. Twenty billion dollars stolen by foreign criminal organizations operating from jurisdictions where American law enforcement has no reach. Countries that don't cooperate with extradition. Countries that don't investigate cybercrime. Countries that might be quietly benefiting from it.

The traditional options were diplomacy, sanctions, and whatever the intelligence community could do in classified programs nobody talks about. The NSPM adds a fourth option: unleash the American private sector.

The memorandum states it plainly. "The American private sector is the most innovative and technologically advanced in the world, and its scale, speed, and capacity secure a critical offensive cyber advantage for the United States." And then: "American businesses' innovative capabilities have historically been underutilized in efforts to identify and disrupt criminal networks operating in cyberspace."

Underutilized. Past tense. That era ended on August 12.

This didn't come out of nowhere. There's a sequence.

On March 6, 2026, the President signed Executive Order 14390 "Combating Cybercrime, Fraud, and Predatory Schemes Against American Citizens." That order directed federal agencies to develop action plans. It created the NCC's operational cell framework. But it stopped short of the critical step: authorizing private companies to act.

Five months later, the NSPM provides that authorization. EO 14390 was the blueprint. The NSPM is the building permit.

And two days before the NSPM was signed, a private crypto exchange called Bybit sued North Korea's Lazarus Group in U.S. federal court and won a preliminary injunction freezing $1.5 billion in stolen assets. A private company, using the American legal system, against a sovereign state's hacking apparatus. The civil version of what the NSPM now authorizes in the operational domain.

Here's what this means for everything else that's been happening.

Treasury designates crypto exchanges used by Iran's Revolutionary Guard and publishes their wallet addresses. OFAC sanctions shadow banking networks. FinCEN assesses $125 million penalties against banks that fail to catch illicit flows. The Enforcement Directorate in India seizes $2.4 billion from a single conglomerate. China sentences defense ministers to death. Russia builds surveillance architecture over its own crypto markets. Nineteen nations form a military coalition in Panama.

All of those are governments acting through government instruments. Sanctions, seizures, indictments, designations, military coalitions.

The NSPM says: that's not enough. The government will also authorize private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against the same criminal networks that everyone else is trying to dismantle through traditional enforcement.

The government built the enforcement architecture. Now it's handing some of the tools to the private sector and saying: help us use them. You're faster. You're more innovative. You're already in the networks. Here's your letter of marque. Go hunting.

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

The natural reading is that Russia is building an escape route. The U.S. keeps shutting down Russian crypto exchanges Garantex in 2025, Grinex's wallets frozen by Tether so Russia built its own regulated market that operates under Russian law, beyond the reach of American sanctions enforcement.

That reading is wrong.

Read the law.

Here's what Russia actually built.

State-registered exchanges. Only organizations entered in a government register can operate. Digital depositories that maintain records of ownership. Investor testing requirements before anyone can trade. Annual caps non-qualified investors can purchase no more than 300,000 rubles, about $4,000, per year per broker. Central Bank oversight of every exchange, custodian, and intermediary.

Every transaction recorded. Every owner known. Every exchange supervised.

Before this law, Russian crypto activity ran through Garantex, Grinex, shadow OTC desks, and Telegram brokers. Those channels were dark. Not just dark to the U.S. Treasury. Dark to Russia. Russian intelligence didn't know what was moving through Russian crypto infrastructure any better than Washington did.

Now they will.

And then there's the line in the law that tells you everything.

Cryptocurrencies are approved for cross-border settlements. They are banned as domestic payment methods.

You can use crypto to move value across borders. You cannot use it to buy anything inside Russia. The law separates the two uses and legalizes only the one that Russia's government wants to monitor international flows.

So what did Russia actually do?

It didn't build an escape route from transparency. It built a surveillance architecture for its own crypto flows. It took the activity that was running through shadows and told it: come inside where we can see you, or you're a criminal under Russian law too.

Think about what this means for the person operating in the dark.

Before the law, a Russian businessman moving money through a Telegram OTC desk was in a gray area. There was no law regulating it, so there was no law to break. He was invisible to Moscow and invisible to Washington.

After the law, that same businessman has a choice. Move onto the registered exchange where the Central Bank sees every transaction, the digital depository records his ownership, and his annual volume is capped and monitored. Or stay in the shadows where he is now breaking Russian law, not just American sanctions.

Before, he was hiding from one government. Now he's hiding from two.

Both sovereigns are squeezing from both sides. The operator who stays in the dark is a criminal in Moscow and in Washington. Not because they coordinated. Because they both built the same thing for their own reasons.

This is what every country covered in this series has been doing.

The United States built the GENIUS Act framework, requiring stablecoin issuers to implement bank-grade know-your-customer rules. Treasury designated crypto exchanges laundering money for Iran and published on-chain wallet addresses so that every participant in the system can screen for sanctioned flows.

India formally designated its Enforcement Directorate as the lead agency for seized cryptocurrency. Its Criminal Investigation Department, with Binance's help, busted a crypto-hawala network linked to Hamas and Houthi organizations.

China is running the largest anti-corruption purge in its history six sectors of its own government, two former defense ministers sentenced to death, the former head of China Development Bank under investigation.

Saudi Arabia's anti-corruption body Nazaha arrests over a hundred officials every month.

Mexico's current Attorney General arrested the former Attorney General. Then she arrested a former governor.

Colombia's new president captured a narcotrafficking commander 48 hours after inauguration.

Syria's first judicial act as a new government was sentencing its former president to death for using the state as a weapon.

And now Russia the country under the most comprehensive sanctions regime in history has built a regulated, supervised, recorded crypto market under its own Central Bank. Not to evade transparency. To impose it. On its own people. For its own purposes.

Every government in the world is doing the same thing.

They are forcing activity out of the dark and onto infrastructure they control. They are building transparent rails. They are telling the people who operate in the shadows: come where we can see you, or you are a criminal. Not because anyone told them to. Because every sovereign has the same interest in knowing where the money is.

The United States wants to see the flows so it can enforce sanctions. Russia wants to see the flows so it can control capital flight and fund its war. China wants to see the flows so it can purge corruption. India wants to see the flows so it can prosecute money laundering. Saudi Arabia wants to see the flows so it can break the old patronage networks.

Different reasons. Same architecture. Same outcome.

The money has nowhere left to hide not because one government closed all the doors, but because every government is closing its own doors, from the inside, for its own reasons.

That's not coordination.
That's convergence.

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

The legal timeline for Brightcom Group Limited’s (BCG) pending appeals before the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) spans multiple contested regulatory directives. 

The tribunal continues to process challenges against both interim and final orders issued by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). 

The primary SAT appeal cases and procedural tracks are detailed below: 

## 1. Main Appeal Track: Case SEBI/0474/2024

* Current Status: This remains the primary active master-case pending before the SAT. 

* Key Milestones: The case has seen multiple iterations of filings and rejoinders between Brightcom and SEBI. Following extensive adjustments and procedural updates across 2024 and 2025, the tribunal actively issued its most recent procedural order on February 19, 2026. 

* Core Subject: This appeal directly challenges SEBI's sweeping enforcement directives concerning systemic financial accounting irregularities, fund diversion via preferential allotments, and fabricated asset representations. [4, 5] 

## 2. Appeals Against the SEBI Confirmatory Order

* The Directive: SEBI issued a Confirmatory Order on February 28, 2024, which solidified restrictions against the company's former top executives. 

* The Timeline: Brightcom pulled back its older interlocutory appeals (such as Appeal No. 942 of 2023) to file a dedicated challenge against this confirmatory text. After successive delays, including an adjournment on April 16, 2025, requested by intervening applicants, the tribunal moved the matter into its late-2025 and 2026 review cycles. 

## 3. Historical SAT Interventions & Rulings

* Denial of Interim Relief: Early in the timeline, SAT strongly refused to grant Brightcom any interim stay or immediate emergency relief. [8, 9] 
* Tribunal Observations: The tribunal noted that prima facie evidence pointed to an explicit diversion of funds concerning at least 22 out of 82 allottees in preferential share allocations. SAT categorically ruled that it found no legal loopholes or flaws in SEBI's strict mandate forcing former CMD Suresh Kumar Reddy and CFO Narayana Raju to step down. 

## Parallel Legal Track: Telangana High Court
It is critical to note that Brightcom’s legal team has heavily cross-filed petitions. While the SAT evaluates market-compliance and penalty details, the Telangana High Court handles active constitutional writ petitions (WP7447/2025 and WP8046/2025) challenging SEBI’s subsequent Final Order dated February 6, 2025, alongside ongoing contempt cases concerning stock exchange trading suspensions. 

------------------------------

The core issue keeping Brightcom Group Limited (BCG) under severe pressure is its persistent legacy of corporate governance failures and a massive regulatory overhang, even though its shares were allowed to resume trading on the NSE and BSE in July 2025.

The primary challenges currently impacting the company include:

1. Regulatory Overhang and Past Legal Orders

* SEBI and ED Scrutiny: The company remains under the shadow of heavy penalties and past orders by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and the Enforcement Directorate (ED). Past probes revealed extensive financial accounting malpractices, round-tripping of funds via subsidiaries, and the siphoning off of over ₹300 crore. 

* Management Restrictions: Under SEBI orders, former promoter/CMD Suresh Kumar Reddy and CFO Narayana Raju remain banned from holding key managerial positions or participating in capital markets. Ongoing appeals and proceedings continue to play out across the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) and the Telangana High Court. 

* Exchange Clarifications: Stock exchanges continue to monitor the company tightly. As recently as February 2026, the Exchange sought fresh clarifications from Brightcom Group due to significant, unexplained movements in its stock price. [7] 

2. High Valuation De-Rating and Market Scepticism

* Deep Valuation Discount: Despite reporting operationally active figures for Q1 FY27 (including a ₹1,750 crore revenue and ₹260 crore net profit), the stock trades at an incredibly depressed Price-to-Earnings (P/E) multiple of just 2.1x. The market refuses to reward the company's financial growth because of lingering trust issues regarding the true quality of its earnings. 

* Low Insider Skin in the Game: The promoter holding remains precariously low at just 18.38%. This leaves very little corporate equity backing, creating high institutional and retail anxiety regarding long-term ownership commitment. [1, 8] 

## 3. Structural Financial Weaknesses

* High Debtor Days: The company suffers from historically high debtor days. This means it takes a long time to collect cash from clients, restricting working capital efficiency and causing cash flow friction despite paper profits. [1] 
* Speculative Volatility: Classified broadly within the highly volatile penny stock spectrum, the share price remains prone to extreme liquidity-driven and sentiment-led price movements rather than stable institutional backing.

UPDATE TO ALL MEMBERS ON LOCUM ENGAGEMENT & CASUALIZATION

The leadership of NARD, ably led by the Strategic P-MUS (Garkuwan Matasan Arewa), is pleased to update members on the outcome of the FMoHSW Committee on  Regulation and Casualization of Doctors.

Following extensive consultations, the Committee has developed a National Policy on the Engagement of Locum, aimed at ensuring fair, transparent and non-exploitative engagement of temporary healthcare personnel.

KEY RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Recruitment & Approval:
   Locum engagement must be based on a clearly identified staffing gap and approved by the appropriate hospital authorities.

2. Contract Duration:
   Initial locum contracts shall not exceed 6 months, with only one additional 6-month renewal permitted. Continuous engagement for 12 months makes the position eligible for permanent appointment.

3. Maximum Work Hours:
   Healthcare personnel shall work a maximum of 48 hours per week, including weekends. Excess hours must be appropriately compensated.

4. Maximum Duty Period:
   No healthcare personnel shall work beyond 24 continuous hours, including call duty.

5. Mandatory Rest:
   
   - Minimum 12 hours between shifts.

   - Mandatory 24-hour post-call rest after weekday and weekend calls.

   - A 1-hour break after 6 hours of continuous work.

6. Call Duty:
   
   - Maximum 2 calls per week.

   - Maximum 1 weekend call per month.

   - Calls must be equitably distributed.

7. Remuneration & Welfare:
Pay rates are standardized in alignment with the government's 
Scheme of Service. Remuneration must be paid monthly without delay, accompanied by monthly 
payslips. 

Locum staff are entitled to all government-approved leaves, public holidays, and occupational insurance coverage.

8. Excess Work Hours:
   Excess hours must be properly documented, monitored and adequately compensated, or appropriately balanced with structured time-off.

9. Protection Against Abuse:
   Locum engagement must not be used as a permanent substitute for substantive recruitment or as a means of exploiting healthcare workers.

10. Integration & Safety: All locum workers must undergo mandatory orientation and integration into their respective clinical or administrative teams. Institutions are required to provide safe 
working environment, adequate call rooms, refreshments during prolonged calls/shifts, and burnout prevention programs.

11. Discipline & Grievance Process: Professional misconduct shall be governed by the regulatory 
council guidelines. Contracts can be terminated by either party with a one-month notice or payment in lieu, and all accrued entitlements must be settled within 14 days of termination. Disputes escalate through institutional mechanisms up to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, and the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment.

12. Monitoring: The Ministry would ensure Institutions do not engage in exploitative staffing practices and violations of this guideline in line with the Nigerian Labour Law.

13. Policy Review and Effective Date:
This policy becomes legally binding on the exact date of approval by the Federal Ministry of 
Health and Social Welfare (FMoH&SW). To ensure its continuous operational relevance, the 
policy mandates a comprehensive evaluation and review within two (2) years of its 
implementation.

The policy is expected to provide a more structured and equitable framework for locum engagement across Nigerian health institutions.

Appreciation to the Hon. Coordinating Minister for Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Mohammad Ali Pate for this approval.

Special appreciation to the Hon. Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Dr. Iziak Adekunle Salako for his guidance and dictation to seeing this through.

Appreciations are also in order to our distinguished NARDites in the Committee for a job well done. Thank you Dr. Kwarshak Kevin Yakubu, the VP 2 of NARD. Thank you Dr. Shuaibu Ibrahim, the Secretary General of NARD.

NARD is particularly proud of this accomplishments and proves once again what we can achieve when we come together as a team.

NARD remains committed to protecting the dignity, welfare, rights and professional interests of every Nigerian doctor.

It is our hope that the National Council on Health will also give their stamp of approval on this.

Dr. Abdulmajid Yahya Ibrahim

text:
Accurately Grasp the New Regulations on Virtual Currencies and RWA Tokens, and Seek New Financing Opportunities on the Basis of Compliance

Tags: Banking and Financing - Fintech

On February 6, 2026, the People's Bank of China and eight other ministries jointly issued the "Notice on Further Preventing and Handling Risks Related to Virtual Currencies" (Yinfa [2026] No. 42, hereinafter referred to as "Document No. 42"). On the same day, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) issued the "Regulatory Guidelines on the Issuance of Asset-Backed Securities Tokens Overseas by Domestic Assets" (CSRC Announcement [2026] No. 1, hereinafter referred to as "CSRC Announcement No. 1"). These two documents established the latest policy framework for the regulation of virtual assets in China.

I. Regulatory Framework and Division of Responsibilities for Virtual Assets The above two documents continue the risk warnings previously issued by seven industry associations, dividing virtual assets into two major categories: virtual currencies and real-world asset (RWA) tokens. Based on this, a policy framework for the classified regulation of virtual assets was constructed. This division is the logical starting point for understanding China's latest regulatory policies. As two types of tokens both backed by underlying assets—stablecoins and RWA tokens—Document No. 42 treats them as two different things, adopting differentiated regulatory policies. As a tokenization of real-world assets, RWA is merely securities and other assets dressed in a token "cloak." Its essence is a financing tool or investment product, a view shared by regulations and regulatory bodies in the United States, Singapore, and Hong Kong. Stablecoins pegged to fiat currencies, however, indirectly fulfill some functions of fiat currencies in circulation. Their essence is a non-yielding payment tool, posing a threat to a country's sovereign currency. The currency substitution effect already observed in some countries with weak currencies proves this point; therefore, their regulation requires greater caution. It is precisely this fundamental difference that has led to different stances in regulatory policies. Virtual currencies, including stablecoins [1], are subject to a "strict prohibition both domestically and internationally" policy; RWA tokens are regulated according to the principle of "strict prohibition domestically and strict management overseas," providing a new option for enterprises to conduct compliant overseas financing.

Based on the above regulatory framework, Document No. 42 divided the responsibilities of various virtual asset regulatory agencies. Virtual currencies are regulated by the People's Bank of China in conjunction with relevant departments; RWA tokens are regulated by the National Development and Reform Commission, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, and the State Administration of Foreign Exchange according to their respective duties.

II. Regulatory Policies on Virtual Currencies

Document No. 42 reiterates the core regulatory principle of strictly prohibiting virtual currencies both domestically and internationally, implementing a comprehensive ban on virtual currencies. While maintaining a strict ban on stablecoins, it retains the possibility of future compliant issuance. Virtual currency-related businesses without compliant operating space will be investigated and dealt with as illegal financial activities.

1. Virtual Currencies: Comprehensive and Strict Prohibition Domestically and Internationally
For ordinary virtual currencies such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tether, which are not pegged to fiat currencies, a strict ban is implemented both domestically and internationally without exception, completely eradicating their breeding ground within the country and blocking the infiltration of overseas businesses into the country.

Negation of Fiat Currency Status: These virtual currencies are issued by non-monetary authorities, exist in digital form based on encryption and distributed ledger technologies, do not have the same legal status as fiat currencies, have no legal tender status, and cannot be used as currency in the domestic market.

Complete Prohibition on Domestic Business: All businesses conducted within China, including the exchange of fiat currency for virtual currency, exchange between virtual currencies, acting as a central counterparty in buying and selling virtual currencies, providing information intermediary/pricing services for virtual currency transactions, token issuance financing, and trading of virtual currency-related financial products, are suspected of illegal token issuance, unauthorized public offering of securities, and illegal operation of securities and futures businesses. All such activities are strictly prohibited and will be resolutely shut down according to law.

Complete Blockade of Services from Overseas to Domestic: Overseas entities and individuals are prohibited from providing any form of virtual currency-related trading, exchange, intermediary, or pricing services to domestic entities, cutting off the channels through which overseas virtual currency business enters the domestic market.

Prohibition on Overseas Issuance by Domestic Entities and Their Controlled Overseas Entities: Without the approval of relevant departments in accordance with laws and regulations, domestic entities and their controlled overseas entities are prohibited from issuing any form of virtual currency (including stablecoins) overseas, blocking the possibility of domestic entities conducting virtual currency-related business through overseas entities. Accordingly, internet platform companies and overseas Chinese-funded financial institutions applying for stablecoin issuance licenses in Hong Kong and other locations must obtain the approval of relevant domestic regulatory departments.

Full-Chain Control

(1) Financial Services: Financial institutions (including non-bank payment institutions) are prohibited from providing financial services such as account opening, fund transfer, and clearing and settlement for virtual currency businesses. They are also prohibited from issuing or selling related financial products and from including them in the scope of collateral or insurance liability.

(2) Marketing, Display, and Promotion: Internet companies are prohibited from providing services such as online business venues, commercial displays, marketing promotion, and paid traffic redirection for virtual currency businesses. Any illegal or irregular clues must be reported promptly and cooperation with regulatory investigations must be provided.

(3) Registration and Advertising: Market supervision departments will include terms such as "virtual currency," "cryptocurrency," and "virtual assets" in the prohibited scope of business entity registration, and will strictly investigate illegal advertisements involving virtual currencies.

(4) Mining: The crackdown on virtual currency "mining" activities will continue, existing mining projects will be completely shut down, and new projects and related services such as the sale of domestic mining machines are strictly prohibited. (5) Legal Liability and Risk Assumption: Those who engage in illegal financial activities related to virtual currencies, or provide services for related businesses, will be subject to legal liability determination, handling, and prosecution by local financial management departments, branches and agencies of the State Council's financial management departments, etc.; if a crime is constituted, the case will be transferred to judicial organs for criminal prosecution. Any unit or individual investing in virtual currencies and related financial products whose related civil legal acts violate public order and good morals are invalid, and losses will be borne by the individual; those suspected of disrupting financial order or endangering financial security will be investigated and dealt with by relevant departments according to law.

2. Stablecoins: Reserved Space for Future Compliant Overseas Issuance While Strictly Prohibiting Stablecoins pegged to fiat currencies are included in the scope of virtual currency regulation and are subject to the aforementioned strict domestic and overseas prohibitions, including but not limited to prohibiting domestic entities and their controlled overseas entities from issuing stablecoins and other virtual currencies overseas.

The People's Bank of China convened a "Coordination Mechanism Meeting on Combating Virtual Currency Trading and Speculation" on November 29, 2025. The meeting pointed out that "stablecoins are a form of virtual currency and currently cannot effectively meet the requirements for customer identification and anti-money laundering, posing a risk of being used for illegal activities such as money laundering, fundraising fraud, and illegal cross-border fund transfers." However, the People's Bank of China is not the only central bank to issue risk warnings about stablecoins. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), often referred to as the central bank of central banks, also pointed out that stablecoins fail to meet the requirements of becoming a pillar of the modern monetary system based on core standards such as "singleness, elasticity, and integrity."

Because stablecoins effectively perform some functions of legal tender in circulation, no domestic or foreign entity (regardless of whether it has Chinese capital backing) may issue stablecoins pegged to the RMB outside of Hong Kong without the consent of relevant departments in accordance with laws and regulations. This policy establishes a "long-arm jurisdiction" principle based on the RMB. Hong Kong's Stablecoin Ordinance also contains similar provisions, prohibiting any entity from issuing stablecoins pegged to the Hong Kong dollar outside of Hong Kong without obtaining a stablecoin issuer license issued by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. While prohibiting stablecoins, the aforementioned regulations also imply another layer of meaning: with the approval of relevant departments, stablecoins pegged to the RMB can be issued overseas. This provides a regulatory basis for piloting offshore RMB stablecoins when conditions are ripe.

Although the phrase "relevant departments" is used here, because stablecoins fulfill some functions of legal tender, their regulation should logically be carried out by the legal tender regulatory authority, namely the People's Bank of China, in conjunction with relevant departments. Combined with the central bank's previous statements, the development of overseas stablecoins will be dynamically assessed, and regulatory rules will be improved based on the assessment results.

III. RWA Token Regulatory Policy Document No. 42 for the first time clearly defined the legal definition of real-world asset (RWA) tokenization and included it in the regulatory scope. CSRC Announcement No. 1 further refined the regulatory requirements for the issuance of asset-backed securities tokens overseas by domestic assets, establishing the overall regulatory principles of prohibition domestically, permission for overseas operation, categorized regulation, and the same business, same risks, and same rules. Regulatory responsibilities are divided according to token business type (bond tokens, equity tokens, ABS tokens), while clarifying full-process control requirements and reserving a clear path for compliant operation.
